title: Tennis
wiki_lead:
Tennis is a racket sport that is played either individually against a single opponent (singles) or between two teams of two players each (doubles). Each player uses a tennis racket strung with a cord to strike a hollow rubber ball covered with felt over or around a net and into the opponent's court. The objective is to manoeuvre the ball in such a way that the opponent is not able to play a valid return. If a player is unable to return the ball successfully, the opponent scores a point.
Tennis can be played by anyone who can hold a racket, including wheelchair users and those who are blind or with low vision, and is played by people at every level of society and across all ages. The original forms of tennis developed in France during the late Middle Ages. The modern form of tennis originated in Birmingham, England, in the late 19th century as lawn tennis. It had close connections to various field (lawn) games such as croquet and bowls as well as to the older racket sport today called real tennis.
The rules of modern tennis have changed little since the 1890s. The two exceptions are the server needing to have one foot on the ground at all times prior to 1961, and the adoption of the tiebreak in the 1970s. In 2006, professional tennis adopted electronic review technology coupled with a point-challenge system known as Hawk-Eye, which has increasingly been succeeded by fully automated Electronic Line Calling (ELC Live) systems.
Tennis has millions of recreational players and is a popular spectator sport worldwide. The four Grand Slam tournaments, also known as "majors", are especially popular and are considered the epitome of competitive tennis. The four Grand Slam tournaments are the Australian Open, played on hardcourts; the French Open, played on red clay courts; Wimbledon, played on grass courts; and the US Open, also played on hardcourts. Tennis was one of the original Olympic sports, and has been consistently part of the Summer Olympic Games since 1988.

History


Predecessors

Historians believe that the game's ancient origin lay in 12th-century northern France, where a ball was struck with the palm of the hand. Louis X of France was a keen player of jeu de paume ("game of the palm"), which evolved into real tennis, and became notable as the first person to construct indoor tennis courts in the modern style. Louis was unhappy with playing tennis outdoors and accordingly had indoor, enclosed courts made in Paris "around the end of the 13th century". In due course this design spread across royal palaces all over Europe. In June 1316 at Vincennes, Val-de-Marne, and following a particularly exhausting game, Louis drank a large quantity of cooled wine and subsequently died of either pneumonia or pleurisy, although there was also suspicion of poisoning. Because of the contemporary accounts of his death, Louis X is history's first tennis player known by name. Another of the early enthusiasts of the game was King Charles V of France, who had a court set up at the Louvre Palace.
The word tennis probably comes from the French term tenez, which can be translated as "hold!", "receive!" or "take!", an interjection used as a call from the server to his opponent. It was popular in England and France, although the game was only played indoors, where the ball could be hit off the wall. Henry VIII of England was a big fan of this game, which is now known as real tennis.
An epitaph in St Michael's Church, Coventry, written c. 1705, read, in part:

During the 18th and early 19th centuries, as real tennis declined, new racket sports emerged in England.
The invention of the first lawn mower in Britain in 1830 is believed to have been a catalyst for the preparation of modern-style grass courts, sporting ovals, playing fields, pitches, greens, etc. This in turn led to the codification of modern rules for many sports, including lawn tennis, most football codes, lawn bowls and others.

grok_lead: Tennis is a racket sport, originally known as lawn tennis, in which two players (singles) or two pairs of players (doubles) compete against each other by striking a felt-covered hollow rubber ball with rackets over a net into the opponent's court, with the objective of preventing the opponent from returning the ball legally. The game is played on a rectangular court measuring 78 feet (23.77 meters) in length and 27 feet (8.23 meters) in width for singles matches, or 36 feet (10.97 meters) for doubles, divided by a net suspended 3 feet (0.914 meters) high at the center. The origins of tennis trace back to the 11th or 12th century in France, where it evolved from " jeu de paume," a handball game played by monks against monastery walls or over a rope, with the name "tennis" likely deriving from the French word "tenez," meaning "take" or "receive," called by the server. Rackets were introduced in the 16th century, and the modern version of lawn tennis emerged in the 1870s in Britain, patented by Major Walter Clopton Wingfield in 1873 as an outdoor pastime on grass courts. The first major tournament, the Wimbledon Championships, was held in 1877 by the All England Club, marking the sport's formal organization, while international growth accelerated with the founding of the International Lawn Tennis Federation (now the International Tennis Federation, or ITF) on March 1, 1913, in Paris, which serves as the global governing body for the sport. Tennis follows a unique scoring system where points are counted as love (0), 15, 30, and 40, with a game won by the first player to reach four points while leading by at least two; sets are typically won by the first to six games with a two-game margin, and matches in professional play are best of three sets for women and doubles or best of five for men in major events. The sport is governed internationally by the ITF, which oversees amateur and junior levels, while professional circuits are managed by the ATP Tour for men, established in 1972 to represent male players and organize over 60 tournaments annually, and the WTA Tour for women, founded in 1973 to promote gender equity and featuring around 50 events each year. The four Grand Slam tournamentsâAustralian Open (since 1905), French Open (Roland Garros, since 1891), Wimbledon (since 1877), and US Open (since 1881)ârepresent the pinnacle of the sport, drawing top professionals and awarding the most prestige and prize money. Globally, tennis has seen surging participation, with over 106 million players worldwide as of 2024, a 25.6% increase in just five years, driven by its accessibility for health, social, and competitive benefits across all ages. Professional tennis also boasts massive audiences, with the WTA Tour reaching a record 1.1 billion viewers in 2024 and the ATP Tour's social media following exceeding 168 million. Recent developments, such as the introduction of off-court coaching effective from January 1, 2025, and the announcement in October 2025 that the ITF will rebrand as World Tennis in 2026, reflect ongoing efforts to modernize the game while preserving its traditions.
